transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me, Doctor. I really appreciate you taking the time. I... well, I suppose I'm here because I've been feeling a little unsettled lately. It's probably nothing to worry about, and I hope I'm not wasting your time, but... even on my better days, when my mood isn't too low, I just can't quite shake this feeling. 

It's mostly at my church and in my neighborhood walking club. I just... I get the sense that some of the people there are watching me. And sometimes it feels like they're putting little messages about me in the church bulletin, or hiding things about me in the way they talk to each other. Does that make sense? I know it sounds a bit silly, and I'm sure they're lovely people, but it just makes me so uncomfortable. Is that the sort of thing I should be telling you?
How long have you been noticing these feelings that people are watching you or talking about you—days, weeks, or longer?

Oh, goodness... well, I suppose it's been a while. I hope I haven't let it go on too long before coming to see you. I'd say... maybe about eleven months now? Yes, almost a year. It's not just the feeling of being watched, either. Sometimes I... well, I hear things, like whispers, and I see those little messages, like I mentioned. And sometimes my thoughts just get so jumbled up, it's hard to keep them straight. I've tried to just ignore it and be a good neighbor, but it's been going on for nearly eleven months. Am I explaining that alright? I hope I'm giving you the right information.
Over these past eleven months, have you had stretches of time when you felt fine mood-wise—not sad, low, or overly high—yet still experienced the sense of being watched or heard whispers?

Yes, doctor, you're exactly right to ask that. I hope I'm remembering this clearly for you... but yes, there was. 

There was a spell of several weeks where my mood was actually quite nice. I was getting dressed properly every morning, eating a bit better, and just... not feeling so weighed down by everything. I was really trying my best to be positive. But... well, even during those good weeks, I still heard my name being spoken when I was alone in the house. And I still couldn't shake the thought that the people at church were hinting about me. 

I tried to just smile and be polite through it all, but the feelings were still there even when I wasn't feeling sad. Is that the kind of thing you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions properly.
Thinking back over the full eleven months, would you say the weeks when your mood was low or unusually good added up to less than half of that time, or more than half?

Oh, that is a very thoughtful question, Doctor. I want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to know. I hate to sound like a bother, or like I'm not trying my best to be cheerful, but... well, if I'm being completely honest, I'd have to say the low mood has been more than half the time. Yes, definitely more than half. 

Really, for most of this whole stretch... that sadness, and feeling a bit guilty for not doing more, and just losing interest in my days... it's just sort of been sitting there in the background. Even during the times when the whispers or those uncomfortable thoughts about the neighbors were a bit quieter, that heavy feeling was still there. 

I hope I'm not complaining too much by saying that. I know I should count my blessings, but does that give you a better picture of how things have been? I just want to make sure I'm being helpful.
During those weeks when your mood was low, did you also notice changes in your sleep, energy level, or ability to concentrate?

Well, let me think about that... I really want to be accurate for you. My sleep has been mostly alright, I suppose, and I try my hardest to keep my mind on what I'm doing. But... oh, I feel silly even mentioning it, because I know I shouldn't be so lazy at my age. 

But my energy... well, it just hasn't been what it should be. Even after I've spent a full night in bed, just doing the simplest things can feel so tiring. Like carrying the laundry basket, or just walking down the driveway to check the mailbox... my body just feels so heavy, almost like I've already put in a full day of hard work before I've even started. 

I try not to let it stop me, and I do push through because I know I need to keep the house tidy. I hope I don't sound like I'm just making excuses for not getting enough done. Is it normal to feel that way when you're feeling down, Doctor? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of details.
Do you drink alcohol, use any recreational drugs, or take medications that affect your mind, and do you have any medical conditions like thyroid problems?

Oh, no, no, Doctor. I wouldn't want you to think I... well, I don't touch alcohol or any kind of drugs like that. I know some people do, and I'm not judging, but I've always tried to live a clean life. And my doctor hasn't given me any strong medications or anything that would mess with my head. 

As for medical problems... well, I try to keep myself in good shape, you know? I haven't been told I have any thyroid issues or anything serious like that. I go to my checkups and everything always seems to be in working order, thankfully. 

I hope that's a relief to hear? I just want to make sure I'm taking care of myself the way I'm supposed to, so you have one less thing to worry about with me. Did I answer that the right way for your notes?

During that several-week stretch when your mood was good, did the whispering and feeling of being watched continue every day without any break, or were there also some days during that time when you didn't notice them at all?

Well, let me think about that good stretch... I want to be as helpful as I can. There was a spell of several weeks where I was actually doing quite well, I think. I was getting dressed nicely every day, eating a bit better, and I didn't feel so... so weighed down by everything. I was really trying my best to keep my spirits up.

But... oh, I feel a little foolish admitting this, because I was doing so much better otherwise. Even during those good weeks, when I was feeling brighter... I still heard my name being whispered in the house. And... well, I still had those thoughts that the people at church were dropping hints about me. 

It wasn't that I wasn't trying to ignore it, Doctor, I really was. I just couldn't quite shake it, even when my mood lifted. I hope it doesn't mean I wasn't making progress during those weeks? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the full picture, even the parts I'm a little embarrassed by. Is that the kind of detail you needed?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports approximately 11 months of continuous psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations of hearing her name whispered, persecutory/referential delusions about church members and neighbors, and thought disorganization). During most of this period, she also experienced a concurrent major depressive syndrome (depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue/low energy) that overlapped with psychotic symptoms for more than half the total illness duration, satisfying the mood-symptom-majority criterion for schizoaffective disorder. Critically, she also described a distinct several-week period of euthymic/improved mood (better grooming, appetite, less sadness) during which the hallucinations and delusional beliefs persisted, confirming psychotic symptoms occurred for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode—the key differentiator from mood disorder with psychotic features. Substance use and general medical/endocrine causes (e.g., thyroid disease) were denied, ruling out substance/medication-induced psychosis and psychotic disorder due to another medical condition. The predominant mood component being depressive (no manic/hypomanic symptoms reported) supports the depressive subtype.
